US to cut nearly $4 billion in Israel military aid, Trump says
November 4, 2026
The US will end an agreement that sees it provide Israel nearly $4 billion (€3.5 billion) in annual aid by the end of the year, President Donald Trump said Tuesday.
In an interview with the conservative US broadcaster Fox, Trump said Israel was "fine" with him ending the assistance, which is due to run until the end of 2028.
"Now, as far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that we give Israel $4 billion a year, and we made a deal months ago that we're stopping," Trump told the hosts of the "Fox & Friends" morning show, referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump said Israel is "fine" with the US slashing the aid.
"We've already agreed that by the end of the year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," the US president said, while adding that Israel can still buy US weapons "whenever they want."
"Israel's our number one; we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it," Trump added.
How much does the US support Israel?
The US provides $3.8 billion to Israel under a 10-year security assistance accord that began in 2019 and was signed by Barack Obama before Trump took office in 2017.
In the Fox News interview, Trump did not elaborate on how the military assistance would end by the end of 2026. The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) that supplies Israel with nearly $4 billion in military aid each year is set to run until September 2028.
The US has backed Israel far more than any other country. Israel has received the inflation-adjusted equivalent of more than $300 billion in US economic and military support since it was founded in 1948, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.
Netanyahu has said previously that he wants to end Israel's reliance on US military support. In June, he said that while he "deeply" appreciates the support Israel has received from its "American friends … we need to break free from dependency and build our own independent armaments network."
Trump's announcement has drawn fierce criticism from Netanyahu's opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, who is vying to form a coalition that can challenge the prime minister.
The leader of the Israeli opposition said Trump's remarks were evidence that Netanyahu must be removed from office.
"The fact that Israel's defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu's conduct is," Eisenkot said in a statement posted on X.
"He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced."
Why did Trump make the remarks on midterm election day?
Trump's surprise comments came as US voters headed to polling stations on Tuesday for the midterm elections, which have been framed as a referendum on Trump's second term and could see his Republican Party lose control of Congress.
Democrats such as Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan have criticized continued US aid to Israel while Americans struggle to keep up with rising prices at home.
The US' unconditional support for Israel, which had been a rare and reliable source of bipartisan consensus for decades, has grown increasingly unpopular with the American public, particularly since Israel's military offensive in Gaza, which came in response to the Hamas terror attack in October 2023.
A Quinnipiac University poll in June found that 48% of all voters and 66% of Democrats think the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16% and 20% in 2017, respectively. A poll by the Pew Research Center in March last year found that 53% of Americans view Israel unfavorably, up from 42% in 2022.
Trump said his move to end aid to Israel was in part meant to counter a "bad talking point" that left-wing Democrats such as El-Sayed have used against Republicans amid rising anti-Israel sentiment in the country over the conflict and humanitarian situation in Gaza.
"Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they (Israel) don't need it (the assistance)?" the US president said on Fox & Friends.
What did Trump say about the war in Iran?
In the same TV interview, Trump also confirmed that US forces attacked Iran overnight.
Trump said the US military hit an Iranian anti-aircraft facility in a "minor" attack.
"They built an anti-aircraft facility... As soon as it was completed, we hit it last night very nicely," Trump told the hosts of the "Fox & Friends" morning show.
The war with Iran, which the US has fought jointly with Israel, has seen US gasoline prices surge and Trump's approval ratings decline sharply as a result.
Jon Alterman of the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank in Washington, told Reuters news agency that the timing of Trump's announcements on Israel and Iran was "curious."
"Why did President Trump announce it on Election Day? And why did he announce it amidst speculation that a major joint US-Israeli military strike against Iran may be days away?"

President Donald Trump on Tuesday said he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that will see the U.S. “cut off” military aid to Israel this year because Republicans “suffer the slings” from Democratic candidates over the issue.
The president’s comments came as voters head to the polls for the last day of voting in the high-stakes midterm elections. The elections could ultimately determine how effective Trump’s agenda is in the back half of his second term.

“Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that — we give Israel $4 billion a year — and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping, and … they’re fine with it because, you know, they’ve become a very successful country. They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying any more,” the president said in an interview on Fox News. “So it’s just a wasted thing because we’ve already agreed that by the end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel.”
Trump did not provide specifics on the forms of military aid that will end, nor how it will be ended.
Trump made the comment after he was asked about the rise of antisemitism, that it appears “the next generation has no interest in providing arms, selling arms to Israel” and that Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is counting on the shift in public opinion regarding U.S. military aid to Israel in his election bid.
El-Sayed, who is in a tight race with Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, has said of Israel that if elected, his responsibility would be Michigan’s children “rather than thinking about what’s in the interest of a foreign government.” He has rejected antisemitism charges during the race.
An ABC News/Washington Post/IPSOS poll last month found 58% of Americans say the U.S. should either reduce military support to Israel or end it completely.
The president said politics influenced the decision to cut aid because he doesn’t want to give Democrats a “talking point” to use against Republicans.
“We were giving them $4 billion. We are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year,” Trump said.
“Why?” Fox’s Brian Kilmeade pressed the president.
“Because they don’t need it, Brian. I mean, I ask them because they don’t need it, and because why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad — it’s a bad talking point because you say, ‘Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?’ Israel’s our number one. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it.”
Trump added that Netanyahu “brought it up” and that it would be “appropriate” to end aid.
Netanyahu has not yet released a public statement on Trump’s comments. Neither the prime minister’s office nor the Israeli Defense Ministry immediately responded to ABC News’ requests for comment.
Trump, when pressed, did not specify if the move meant was the U.S no longer giving military equipment or money, but suggested it was part of an effort to balance the federal budget.
The vast majority of U.S. military aid to Israel is governed by a 10-year memorandum of understanding between the countries. The current agreement, which was negotiated and signed toward the end of the Obama administration, is set to expire at the end of fiscal year 2028.
Two sources at Israel’s Finance Ministry, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on the record, expressed surprise at Trump’s comments, with one highlighting the Obama-era MoU and the other noting that the future annual budget had already been drafted based on the current agreement.
Under the current MoU, the U.S. provides Israel with $3.8 billion in support annually. Much of that — $3.3 billion — is Foreign Military Financing (FMF) — which is money primarily designated for the purchase of U.S.-manufactured defense equipment. Per the terms of the deal, Israel is required to spend 92% of its FMF on U.S.-made defense products in 2026 and 2027, and 100% of it on American goods in 2028.
MoUs are not legally binding agreements, but Congress effectively codified the annual FMF support levels stipulated by the current deal with Israel as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 — a measure that had bipartisan support at the time it was passed into law.
Netanyahu has publicly called for the phasing out of U.S. military aid for Israel, arguing that the country doesn’t need the assistance anymore and expressing a preference for joint investments instead. It is unclear if he would support an abrupt cancellation of the current MoU.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival in last week’s Israeli election, responded to Trump’s announcement in a statement on Tuesday evening local time, saying that his country’s “special relationship with the United States is a key component in its national security.”
“The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger,” he said. “We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”
Eisenkot said Netanyahu “must provide answers to Israeli citizens” immediately.
The final vote count from last Tuesday’s parliamentary election showed that Netanyahu’s bloc maintained its lead, securing 53 seats in the next Knesset, but no coalition secured a 61-seat majority.
The opposition bloc led by Eisenkot won 48 seats, according to official Central Elections Committee figures released on Thursday after all votes had been counted.

sources.news_title: What Trump's Drastic Reduction Of U.S. Military Aid To Israel Could Mean
sources.text:
By the end of the year, the U.S. will stop providing Israel with billions of dollars in annual assistance, President Donald Trump proclaimed Tuesday morning. The announcement was delivered as both Washington and Jerusalem are mulling plans for a new wave of attacks on Iran and amid increasing American voter antipathy toward the Israel in the wake of the Gaza war and America’s involvement in the war with Iran.
While Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin “Bibi” Netanyahu has openly discussed weaning his country off direct U.S. assistance in favor of more cooperation on weapons development, the Trump announcement still caught many there by surprise. It also raises a lot of questions about Congressional authorization and the impact on future sales of advanced arms from U.S. manufacturers, many of which are planned, that still have to be answered.
“As far as paying Israel, Bibi Netanyahu and I have made a deal that – we give Israel $4 billion a year – and we made a deal months ago that we’re stopping,” Trump told Fox & Friends Tuesday morning during his message to American voters going to the polls for the midterm election. “And they’re fine with it because you know they have become a very successful country. They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying anymore to Israel, so it’s just a wasted thing because we’ve already agreed that by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel.”
“Now we’ll help Israel if they need it,” the American leader added. “You know they’ve been a great ally, and we’ve been the greatest of all allies to many many countries.”
Trump did not elaborate on what specific expenditures he was referring to, and we’ve reached out to the White House for more details. However, the president was almost certainly talking about the ongoing decade-long Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Israel.
The MoU calls for providing $3.8 billion in annual aid and it is drawing to a close. Set to run through 2028, the vast majority of that funding is for Foreign Military Financing (FMF) to purchase weaponry mostly from American manufacturers.
“In 2016, the U.S. and Israeli governments signed their third 10-year Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on military aid, covering [Fiscal Year] 2019 to [Fiscal Year] 2028,” according to a 2025 Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. “Under the terms of the MOU, the United States pledged to provide—subject to congressional appropriation—$38 billion in military aid ($33 billion in Foreign Military Financing (FMF) grants plus $5 billion in missile defense appropriations) to Israel.”
The MoU is merely a promise and not legally binding. Congress has to approve any funding requests.
A New Deal
Washington and Jerusalem began negotiating a new MoU in June, according to the Israeli Defense Ministry (MoD).
“The new framework, reflecting the strategic vision of Israel’s Prime Minister and Minister of Defense, is designed to strengthen the IDF’s qualitative military edge through expanded joint investment in research, development, and co-production, deepen the U.S.-Israel partnership demonstrated during Operation Roaring Lion, and gradually transition from aid to a completely reciprocal partnership,” MoD explained.
Netanyahu has been warning Israel for months that it would have to face reduced assistance from the U.S.
“If you think we will continue receiving what I secured twice — tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defense budget — you’d better prepare yourselves and get used to the idea that this will not continue,” he told Israeli media last month, according to Bloomberg News. “That is because America has changed, not because Israel has changed. It will end. It is only a matter of time.”
Netanyahu added that Israel has two more years with Trump, but must prepare for a less favorable Washington after he leaves power.
In January, the Israeli leader said he wanted to reduce Israel’s reliance on American aid. He told The Economist that he was not seeking the full renewal of the MoU, which has to be renegotiated by 2028.
“I want to taper off the military aid within the next 10 years,” Netanyahu told the publication. Asked if he meant “to taper it off to zero,” Netanyahu said “yes.”
“We want to be as independent as possible,” the Israeli leader proffered. Referring to his meeting with the the American president in Florida in late December, Netanyahu added: “In my visit to President Trump, I said we very deeply appreciate the military aid that America has given us over the years, but here too we’ve come of age, and we’ve developed incredible capacities.”
For Israel, the MoU “now matters less for the money it provides than for what it signifies: a gauge of the depth and durability of U.S. support,” the Crisis Group think tank argued in August. “To be sure, FMF has enabled Israel to build up its military power without fully bearing the cost, and phasing out this assistance would impose real burdens. Israel would have to pay for critical U.S. weapons from its own budget.”
However, with its annual GDP now exceeding $700 billion and defense spending above $40 billion, “Israel has found increasing difficulty in arguing that it requires an additional $3.3 billion each year for military purchases,” Crisis Group posited. “Netanyahu has asked the finance ministry to allocate billions of dollars in additional funding for the defense budget over the next decade, a large portion of which would be earmarked to procure U.S. fighter jets, on the assumption that Israel will no longer receive the funds necessary for these purchases from Washington.”
Since the attack by Hamas, U.S. money from the MoU has made up a smaller percentage of the Israeli MoD’s overall budget as the country has increased its own defense spending. Those funds have also been bolstered by several large tranches of U.S. supplemental aid to procure bombs and other weapons.
“For most of the last 15 years, the $3.3 billion Israel receives annually in FMF made up roughly 20% of Israel’s defense budget, which was itself 5-6% of Israel’s GDP in the same period,” the Israel Policy Forum (IPF) explained in May. “Both Israeli defense spending and the share coming from U.S. aid slowly declined amid major economic growth throughout the 2010s, and then spiked in 2023 following the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel and ensuing wars.”
IPF stated that after the Hamas incursion, “Israel sharply increased defense spending (both within the regular budget framework and in extraordinary expenditures) to 8-9% of GDP, and the U.S. gave Israel several large supplemental security assistance packages between late 2023 and early 2026 in addition to the MOU-directed security aid.”
“The net result, taking into account both much higher Israeli spending and large amounts of American aid, is that in 2024 U.S. assistance briefly accounted for more than one third of Israel’s defense budget,” IPF noted. “In 2025 this figure dropped to close to 10%, with Israel spending an estimated NIS 168 billion ($52 billion) on defense in that year.”
Until recently, “Israel had been given a partial exemption” on the requirement that FMF funds be allocated for American products,” the Crisis Group noted. This allowed Israel to “invest a portion of the money in its own defense industry, Crisis Group explained. “This carveout, in turn, has made Israeli firms more competitive in the arms export market.”
Heavy Reliance On American Hardware
Israel, which has received more than $175 billion in U.S. aid since its creation in 1948, relies heavily on American weaponry. The Israeli Air Force (IAF) tactical aviation fleet consists of U.S.-built F-15s, F-16s, F-35s and AH-64 Apache attack helicopters, among other U.S. types. Israel also made deals for a number of other platforms including KC-46A aerial refueling tankers and CH-53K heavy-lift helicopters and it uses large amounts of American precision munitions. Meanwhile, Israeli missile defense systems like Iron Dome and Arrow 3 have been developed with significant assistance from the U.S.
A top Israeli MoD official told The Times of Israel (ToI) last month that his country wants to flip the switch to add value to the American defense industry by using its experience developing weapons as it fights seemingly constant wars. The continual threats from regional actors and terror groups allow Israel to serve as a testing ground for U.S. defense technologies, Aviram Hasson, director of the Defense Ministry’s mission to the US and Canada, explained.
“Hasson pointed to engineering breakthroughs and intellectual property emerging through development of Israel’s active-defense systems, saying every US government request for technology arising from the long-range anti-ballistic missile Arrow 3 program has been fulfilled,” the publication noted.
“It is clear on both sides of the ocean that this cooperation is a strategic need of both powers, not only of Israel,” Hasson told ToI.
U.S. Has Paid Far More Than $4B A Year For Israel’s Defense
Beyond direct financial aid, the U.S. has expended a great deal of resources defending Israel over the past several years. This has included defending against multiple Iranian missile barrages on Israel on top of participating directly in two wars. In addition, there were the constant drone and missile battles in the Red Sea with the Houthis, who began attacking shipping there in response to Israel’s war in Gaza. Part of the U.S. operation against the Houthis was also providing a layer of protection against long-range missile and drone launches at Israel by the rebel group.
During the course of all these events, the U.S. deployed a very large number of its available warships, aircraft, and air defenses, as well as thousands of personnel, to the Middle East at great expense, both in dollars and the toll on troops and equipment.
Just this year alone, 23 U.S. troops have died and nearly 900 have been injured since the launch of Epic Fury in February. Dozens of aircraft have been destroyed and U.S. bases in the region have been partially destroyed and will take billions to repair.
The U.S. has also fired off a large amount of its own munitions defending Israel from attacks by Iran and its proxies. This has contributed heavily to shortfalls in America’s own stockpiles.
All told, the U.S. has spent nearly $50 billion just on the most current conflict with Iran, far exceeding the $4 billion Israel gets per year in annual direct aid. Then there is the opportunity cost of the massive wear and tear on the force and the U.S. military’s overall capacity to fight in the near and medium term due to all these engagements.
All that being said, it can be argued that the U.S. had major interests in participating in these conflicts beyond just the defense of Israel. It is rarely just that simple. The Iran nuclear program, for instance, has impacts much farther than the Middle East and Israel. Still, the U.S. has poured unprecedented resources into Israel’s defense and these investments far eclipse the $4B being discussed today.
Surprise In Israel
Many Israeli government officials were caught completely off guard by the Trump announcement, according to Politico.
“Officials in the Finance Ministry say they were surprised by U.S. President Donald Trump’s announcement that military aid to Israel would cease by the end of the year, ” the publication reported.
“No formal document was submitted from the Prime Minister’s Office regarding the end of aid,” Politico added. “The ministry was aware of the intention to end it, but was surprised by the intention to do so immediately.”
Officials in the Defense Ministry and the military were also reportedly surprised by the announcement, according to the Post.
“We did not expect this announcement, certainly not today,” a senior defense official told Israeli media.
“There is ongoing dialogue with the Americans, and we can say that we were surprised. We will study the implications of the decision, which has yet to reach professional officials,” the official is quoted as saying.
As for Netanyahu, he has yet to weigh in on Trump’s statement. However, one of his main rivals in the closely fought Israeli parliamentary election that could unseat him has commented.
“The fact that Israel’s defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct is,” Gadi Eisenkot said in a statement. “He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced.”
In his comments to Fox & Friends, Trump conceded that the midterm election played a role in his decision.
The annual assistance to Israel is a “bad talking point” for Democrats, including Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, the president proclaimed.
“The left uses the $4 billion payment … as a signal of unfairness. And we can’t allow that to happen,” Trump stated. “I don’t like that. … It’s almost too easy to target
There are many unknowns surrounding Trump’s statement about diminishing U.S. support for Israel.
The MoU, if that is what he is talking about, still has two years left, and almost $8 billion worth of anticipated funding, the vast majority earmarked for procurement of U.S. arms.
As we noted at the top of this piece, the MoU itself isn’t legally binding but the aid is authorized by law and appropriated by Congress each year. Ending it early would mean Congress either not appropriating the money or changing the law.
Will Congress agree to cut the deal off by December? What about the U.S. defense industry? It is unclear at the moment how, or if, this move would affect American defense contractors selling arms to Israel. These companies depend in large measure on predictability and taking this agreement off the table two years early could be problematic.
It is not exactly clear at this point which U.S. arms makers will be hit the hardest by Trump’s announcement. There are billions of dollars in contracts for the future procurement of aircraft, munitions and other equipment to companies like Boeing for F-15Is and KC-46As, Lockheed Martin for F-35Is and AM General for Joint Light Tactical Vehicles. While Israel has bumped up its defense budget, it is not really known at this point how it will cover these costs without that lost U.S. aid.

"Now we'll help Israel if they need it," Trump said. "Israel is a very thriving country. They don't need it."
The announcement came as Americans voted in crucial midterm elections that will determine control of Congress for the last two years of Trump's presidency, and soon after parliamentary elections in Israel that did not produce a clear winner.

The debate over support for Israel, which divides both Democrats and Republicans, is raging in El-Sayed's home state of Michigan, where there is a large Muslim community.
If he wins, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim member of the U.S. Senate.
He has been a vocal critic of the U.S. alliance with Israel, calling for a halt to aid to the country.
His criticism of Israel was one factor behind Sunday's unexpected endorsement by Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens — El-Sayed's main rival in the party's primary — of his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, illustrating divisions within the party on the issue.

In anticipation of the possible reduction of US financial support in the coming years, the US House this past summer passed a defence bill provision that would deepen US-Israeli military technology ties.

They don’t need it, and we won’t be paying any more,” the president said in an interview on Fox News. “So it’s just a wasted thing because we’ve already agreed that by the end of this year, we won’t be paying Israel.”
Trump did not provide specifics on the forms of military aid that will end, nor how it will be ended.
Trump made the comment after he was asked about the rise of antisemitism, that it appears “the next generation has no interest in providing arms, selling arms to Israel” and that Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is counting on the shift in public opinion regarding U.S. military aid to Israel in his election bid.
El-Sayed, who is in a tight race with Republican former Rep. Mike Rogers, has said of Israel that if elected, his responsibility would be Michigan’s children “rather than thinking about what’s in the interest of a foreign government.” He has rejected antisemitism charges during the race.
An ABC News/Washington Post/IPSOS poll last month found 58% of Americans say the U.S. should either reduce military support to Israel or end it completely.
The president said politics influenced the decision to cut aid because he doesn’t want to give Democrats a “talking point” to use against Republicans.
“We were giving them $4 billion. We are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year,” Trump said.
“Why?” Fox’s Brian Kilmeade pressed the president.
“Because they don’t need it, Brian. I mean, I ask them because they don’t need it, and because why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad — it’s a bad talking point because you say, ‘Why don’t we give everybody $4 billion?’ Israel’s our number one. We give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it.”
Trump added that Netanyahu “brought it up” and that it would be “appropriate” to end aid.
Netanyahu has not yet released a public statement on Trump’s comments. Neither the prime minister’s office nor the Israeli Defense Ministry immediately responded to ABC News’ requests for comment.
Trump, when pressed, did not specify if the move meant was the U.S no longer giving military equipment or money, but suggested it was part of an effort to balance the federal budget.
The vast majority of U.S. military aid to Israel is governed by a 10-year memorandum of understanding between the countries. The current agreement, which was negotiated and signed toward the end of the Obama administration, is set to expire at the end of fiscal year 2028.
Two sources at Israel’s Finance Ministry, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on the record, expressed surprise at Trump’s comments, with one highlighting the Obama-era MoU and the other noting that the future annual budget had already been drafted based on the current agreement.
Under the current MoU, the U.S. provides Israel with $3.8 billion in support annually. Much of that — $3.3 billion — is Foreign Military Financing (FMF) — which is money primarily designated for the purchase of U.S.-manufactured defense equipment. Per the terms of the deal, Israel is required to spend 92% of its FMF on U.S.-made defense products in 2026 and 2027, and 100% of it on American goods in 2028.
MoUs are not legally binding agreements, but Congress effectively codified the annual FMF support levels stipulated by the current deal with Israel as part of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 — a measure that had bipartisan support at the time it was passed into law.
Netanyahu has publicly called for the phasing out of U.S. military aid for Israel, arguing that the country doesn’t need the assistance anymore and expressing a preference for joint investments instead. It is unclear if he would support an abrupt cancellation of the current MoU.
Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu’s main rival in last week’s Israeli election, responded to Trump’s announcement in a statement on Tuesday evening local time, saying that his country’s “special relationship with the United States is a key component in its national security.”
“The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger,” he said. “We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”
Eisenkot said Netanyahu “must provide answers to Israeli citizens” immediately.

Gadi Eisenkot, a political rival seeking to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said the fact that Israeli security officials and citizens learnt about the decision through the media showed how poorly the government had handled the country's relationship with Washington.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump announced Tuesday that the US would soon cut off military aid to Israel.
Trump just said he was ending aid to Israel. He might actually mean it.
The president says American aid to Israel is more trouble than it’s worth. Some right-wing Israelis agree.
During an Election Day interview with Fox & Friends, Trump said of Israel, “We were giving them $4 billion but it’s cut off at the end of the year.”
When asked to explain this position, Trump said that Israel was a “very successful country” that didn’t need Americans’ money — and that the aid had become an “easy target” for “lunatics like [Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul] El-Sayed” in the midterm elections. Trump also suggested that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed with this reasoning and supported a cessation of US aid to his country.
Of course, Trump says a lot of things. If all of his policy declarations could be taken at face value, then US soldiers would now be patrolling the streets of Gaza, while American hoteliers redeveloped its coastline.
Further, Trump’s remarks Tuesday morning seem to have been ad-libbed. The Israeli Treasury Department reportedly had no knowledge of a supposed joint agreement to end US aid. And existing US law provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual funding through 2028.
All this said, Trump didn’t pluck his Election Day rant out of thin air. Rather, his remarks actually reflect a prominent strain of thinking among Israeli leaders and security experts. In their view, America’s cash may no longer be worth the political blowback that it invites.
Given this Israeli sentiment — and the souring of American public opinion toward Israel — the United States might very well draw down aid in the near future (although, probably not as soon as “the end of the year”).
The Israeli case against US aid to Israel
During a May interview with 60 Minutes, Netanyahu said he would like to “draw down to zero the American financial support, the financial component of the military cooperation that we have.”
Amit Halevi, a lawmaker in Israel’s parliament and member of Netanyahu’s party, spelled out the logic of his position last year. In a pamphlet outlining his vision for the US-Israel relationship, Halevi said US military aid “creates a false narrative of dependency, weakens Israel’s global standing and subjects it to political pressure.” Halevi met with the leadership of the Heritage Foundation — arguably, the GOP’s most influential think tank — in 2025, shortly after Heritage had released its own controversial call for the (very gradual) phasing out of US aid to Israel.
Many on the Israeli right believe that such aid compromises Israeli sovereignty. As the retired Israel Defense Forces general Amir Avivi told Breitbart in 2024, aid “puts on Israel lots of restrictions,” which prevent it from pursuing its security interests with a free hand. Similar concerns have been voiced by former Israeli Prime Minster Naftali Bennet and ex-Israeli ambassador to Israel Michael Oren.
Their argument boils down to two observations:
- There are many forms of US support that Israel would struggle to do without — but financial aid is not one of them.
- Direct financial aid provokes political blowback in a way that other, more essential forms of US assistance do not.
There is evidence for both these points. In 2025, Israel spent about 7.9 percent of its GDP on the IDF. To sustain its 2025 level of military funding — without American cash — Israel would need to dedicate 8.5 percent of GDP to its military. This might irritate Israel’s taxpayers. But it would scarcely threaten Israel’s ability to pursue whatever foreign policy it sees fit.
By contrast, Israel does need access to American military hardware. It has the money to fund its own military. But to adequately provision it, Israel must be allowed to purchase American-made fighter jets, among myriad other forms of martial technology. And the Israelis would also have a tough time doing without its broad military, diplomatic, and intelligence alliance with the United States.
That alliance has attracted some criticism on the American left and right this year — particularly, after the US partnered with Israel to launch a war against Iran.
But Israel’s American critics seem to have found the aid issue uniquely politically potent. Which makes sense: A voter doesn’t need to have any strong opinion about the Israel-Palestine conflict to oppose sending billions of dollars to a wealthy foreign country. Unlike proposals for an arms embargo or sanctions, cutting off aid speaks directly to Americans’ material interests; that money could be going to US citizens but is flowing to the Israeli military instead.
In his Senate race, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has tried to tap into this isolationist sentiment, describing his plans for slashing aid to Israel — and increasing benefits for US citizens — as an “America First” agenda.
Meanwhile, in a controversial ad, an outside group supporting El-Sayed’s candidacy made this argument in blunter terms, portraying a couple forced to pare back their grocery list, in order to save enough money for “killing Palestinians.”
US aid to Israel is not actually responsible for Americans’ rising grocery bills (although, the war in Iran plausibly is). But the broader isolationist argument has wide resonance. In a recent survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, a majority of Americans favored either reducing or ending aid to Israel. And whether or not Trump’s aid comments referred to a solid plan, his political aides swiftly used them to reclaim the “America First” banner from Democrats like El-Sayed.
Faced with these dynamics, it isn’t hard to see how an Israeli leader might think it best to beat a strategic retreat on financial aid.
A phase-out of US aid may be coming, whether Israel likes it or not
To be clear, Israel’s leadership is by no means united in favor of Trump’s impromptu proposal. Indeed, even those who support winding down US aid have insisted that this withdrawal of financial backing must be gradual. And Gadi Eisenkot, the man most likely to become Israel’s next prime minister, is a staunch advocate for indefinite US aid. On Tuesday, Eisenkot assailed Netanyahu for his purported agreement with Trump about winding down such assistance. Both Israeli leaders are currently trying to cobble together a parliamentary majority through alliances with small political parties, after each failed to win such a majority outright in Israel’s recent elections.
Still, it is quite plausible that Netanyahu genuinely told Trump that he was open to phasing out US aid, given the Israeli prime minister’s public remarks on that subject.
In any case, authority over US spending ultimately lies with the American people’s elected representatives, not Israeli officials. On the US left, right, and center, political winds are blowing against aid to Israel. With some of that country’s own leaders and admirers bowing to such gusts, the draw down of American aid to Israel might now be a matter of when, not if.

sources.news_title: Trump's big announcement on Israel means nothing
sources.text:
On the morning of Election Day, Donald Trump went on Fox & Friends to deliver a surprise announcement: The United States, he said, would be cutting off $4 billion in aid to Israel at the end of the year.
This was a recognition that supporting Israel has become utterly politically toxic, and perhaps a last-minute attempt to grasp for votes in an increasingly anti-Israel Republican party—but, weapons trade experts say, Trump’s announcement doesn’t actually indicate the United States will stop funding Israel’s wars. Instead, it might mean that the flow of US military aid to Israel will continue in a less trackable form.
“Like, look at the Middle East. I have total control,” Trump said on Fox & Friends this morning. “We have a helper, and it’s Israel because, you know, we are the big, they are the small.”
He went on to assert that a $4 billion payment to Israel would cease at the end of the year, but—even when pressed repeatedly—did not say whether that meant military aid or cash. And he said that the US would continue selling weapons to Israel.
“[Israel is] fine with it because they’ve become a very successful country,” Trump said. “They don’t need it. And we won’t be paying anymore…we won’t be paying Israel. We’ll help Israel if they need it.”
This announcement doesn’t mean the end of US taxpayer dollars financing Israeli wars. “We’re obviously not going to be zeroing out aid,” explained Matt Duss of the Center for International Policy, a former Bernie Sanders aide. “The plan is to rename and reprogram that aid as ‘joint defense partnerships,’ and tuck it into the defense budget.”
Months ago, Congress was already considering phasing out straightforward financial aid to Israel, and instead reframing American spending on Israel as a legally mandated defense industrial partnership, as Americans sour on directly sending taxpayer dollars to the country. A bill currently in the Senate would “establish a cooperative program, with the concurrence of Israel’s Ministry of Defense (MOD), to develop and deploy advanced technologies for countering unmanned systems that threaten the United States and Israel.” Senators will debate the bill after the midterm elections. Trump was likely referring to that repackaging of aid as cooperative weapons development on Fox & Friends, but he didn’t clarify exactly what he meant.
“Consider it barter, military aid or cash,” he said.
In the past, joint US-Israeli military ventures have included projects like Israel’s Iron Dome missile shield. And in June of this year, negotiations for a new memorandum of understanding on joint weapons development with Israel began, as the present memorandum expires in 2028. Amid unprecedented US public opposition to Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in January suggested Israel should “taper off” direct US military assistance over the following decade. But in its place, Netanyahu proposed a joint weapons research and development model. In the end, Duss said, this setup means “American taxpayers will almost certainly be paying more money, but with even less congressional oversight.”
So Trump’s announcement is more of a public relations move to provide a rhetorical defense against some Democratic talking points, as opposed to a real policy. Trump himself said as much: “The left uses the $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, when it’s no secret, as a, as a signal of unfairness, and we can’t allow that to happen.”
“What’s notable here is Trump’s acknowledgement that aid to Israel is a politically losing issue,” Duss said. “He’s acknowledging that this is dragging the Republicans down.”
In the two years after October 7, the US sent at least $21.7 billion in military aid to Israel, according to a paper by William Hartung, research fellow at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, and the Costs of War Project at Brown University. Hartung told Mother Jones that Netanyahu—a staunch ally of Trump’s—might not be thrilled with the timing of this announcement.
“Netanyahu…would not want to do it this quickly,” Hartung said. Netanyahu did endorse the idea of transitioning from a direct-aid model to joint weapons development, “but he wanted it phased in by 10 years from now.”
Trump is still bombing Iran as part of a war conducted alongside Israel: As The Wall Street Journal reported, the Pentagon struck Iran’s Qeshm Island Monday. He may also escalate that war after the midterms, though he told Axios Monday he’s in “no rush” to do so. But in terms of direct aid to Israel, Hartung said,”[Trump] doesn’t like the Democrats using this as a talking point. He is transactional. He’s got this ‘what’s in it for me’ mentality.”
That mentality might be why Trump announced the $4 billion aid cutoff Tuesday morning as part of his final election pitch. “You know, it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target,” Trump said, naming Michigan senatorial candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who has campaigned on ending unconditional military aid to Israel. “Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it? It is a bad talking point.”
But Hartung said Trump’s announcement, delivered as Americans are headed to the polls, isn’t likely to have much electoral impact. “I didn’t expect him to do it on Election Day. If he wanted to have an impact, it’s getting a little late.”

sources.news_title: Trump Announces $4 Billion Israel Aid Cutoff — And Says Netanyahu Asked For It – 100PercentFedUp.com – by Isaac
sources.text:
President Trump just announced a major change in one of America’s longest-running foreign-aid relationships: roughly $4 billion a year in U.S. assistance to Israel is set to end after 2026.
Trump is keeping the alliance while rewriting who pays the bill.
It is a shift from American taxpayers financing the relationship to Israel purchasing the American military equipment it wants — and Trump says Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu raised the idea himself.
Fox News reported that Trump made the announcement during an Election Day call to “Fox & Friends.” He said the support — which he described as military hardware, cash, or barter — “gets cut off at the end of the year.”
Trump said he and Netanyahu reached the understanding months ago after discussing the issue for several years. According to the president, Netanyahu initiated the conversation and said it would be appropriate for Israel to stop receiving the assistance.
The timing was unmistakably political. Trump pointed to Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s attacks on U.S. support for Israel and argued that ending the payment removes an easy Democratic talking point.
Trump said Israel is a thriving country that no longer needs the payment. He also made clear that the alliance and the ability to buy American weapons will remain intact.
“They can buy whatever they want,” Trump said.
That distinction is the heart of the story.
Trump is separating friendship from dependency. Israel can remain a close strategic partner without receiving an automatic multibillion-dollar transfer from American taxpayers every year.
BREAKING: President Trump says the U.S. will end roughly $4 billion in annual aid to Israel by the end of the year, revealing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to the decision.
“Because they don’t need it,” Trump said during an exclusive interview on @foxandfriends, describing Israel as a thriving country that no longer requires American financial assistance.
Trump also said Netanyahu raised the idea of ending the aid himself. He emphasized that Israel remains one of America’s most reliable allies as the two countries prepare for a major shift in their financial relationship.
— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 3, 2026
The current arrangement traces back to a deal signed under Barack Obama.
The State Department says the 2016 memorandum committed the United States to $38 billion in security assistance for fiscal years 2019 through 2028. That breaks down to $3.3 billion in annual Foreign Military Financing and $500 million a year for cooperative missile-defense programs.
The agreement was the largest bilateral military-assistance pledge in U.S. history when it took effect. The missile-defense portion supports joint systems that have included Iron Dome, David’s Sling, Arrow II, and Arrow III.
The package was negotiated by the Obama administration but entered its ten-year funding period during Trump’s first term. It represented a long bipartisan commitment, not a yearly favor created by the current White House.
It also explains why Trump’s “roughly $4 billion” figure is accurate shorthand. The existing package totals $3.8 billion per year before any additional emergency or supplemental funding.
A State Department security-cooperation fact sheet explains that Foreign Military Financing gives Israel access to American systems such as the F-35 and supports purchases through U.S. foreign-military-sales and commercial channels. Israel has also used those channels for heavy-lift helicopters, aerial-refueling tankers, precision-guided munitions, services, and training.
The fact sheet says Israel had hundreds of active Foreign Military Sales cases worth tens of billions of dollars as of late 2023. Those purchases can take years to manufacture and deliver, so ending annual grants does not instantly erase the existing defense pipeline.
The old agreement also phases out Israel’s ability to spend part of the financing on Israeli-made equipment. By 2028, the annual Foreign Military Financing allocation was supposed to be spent entirely through eligible American channels.
Much of the aid therefore cycled back into the American defense industry.
Trump’s announced model goes one step further: Israel would use its own money to buy what it needs.
That is an unmistakably America First arrangement. Keep the alliance, keep the defense trade, and stop treating a wealthy partner as a permanent aid recipient.
There are still important implementation questions.
The existing memorandum runs through 2028, and Congress controls appropriations. Trump did not release a written termination agreement during the interview, and Netanyahu’s office had not immediately published its own detailed account of the change.
Those facts do not erase what the president announced. They mean the next step is turning the announcement into the appropriations, notices, and contracts required to make it real.
The Congressional Research Service previously warned that ending Foreign Military Financing would affect existing weapons contracts as well as future purchases. Israel could have to fund those contracts itself, find other financing, or renegotiate obligations that extend beyond a single budget year.
CRS noted that U.S. financing lets Israel stretch payments for major weapons purchases across multiple years. Contracts already signed can remain in the production queue long after the original appropriation, creating potential termination costs for both governments if a deal is simply canceled.
The report also said Israeli leaders had already discussed weaning the country off American security aid. Israel was considering a substantial increase in its own defense spending, while both governments were weighing what a future security arrangement should look like after the current memorandum expires.
That background makes Trump’s announcement less sudden than it sounds. The abrupt element is his year-end timetable, which arrives two years before the existing memorandum’s scheduled 2028 finish.
That is precisely why the new relationship matters.
This goes beyond a symbolic line-item cut. If completed as Trump described, it changes who pays the bill while preserving Israel’s ability to purchase American defense systems.
This would be a start, but…
1) It’s pennies on the dollar. We’ve spent over $50 billion on the War with Iran on behalf of Israel.
2) The same American taxpayer funds will just flow through as military assistance/coordination instead of as a separate line item in the appropriations bills.
3) They spent $30 million against me because I was the only remaining Republican to oppose this foreign aid.
You’d have to be a fool to think they’re going to end this. It’s a desperate Election Day lie.
— Thomas Massie (@RepThomasMassie) November 3, 2026
Rep. Thomas Massie immediately challenged the announcement, arguing that federal support could simply reappear under different programs.
That skepticism puts a useful marker on the table: the public should watch the actual appropriations and defense agreements. A renamed funding stream would fall short of the change Trump described.
But Trump’s stated direction is still clear. A prosperous ally should pay its own way, and America’s support does not have to mean an endless taxpayer-funded allowance.
That is a significant reset — and one that could become a model for how Trump handles other wealthy American partners.
The alliance remains, and the weapons relationship remains.
What changes is the assumption that U.S. taxpayers must always pick up the tab.

sources.news_title: Trump says U.S. cutting $3.8 billion annual security assistance to Israel
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday (November 3, 2026) that Washington is ending a 10-year security assistance accord with Israel that allowed $3.8 billion in annual assistance to its ally until 2028.
Mr. Trump said Israel was “fine” with him ending the assistance, which began in 2019 and was signed under his predecessor, Barack Obama, three years earlier.
“We’ll help Israel if they need it,” Mr. Trump added in an interview on “Fox and Friends,” saying that he had agreed with Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to cut the assistance.
“Israel’s our number one; we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it... If they did need it, I would say keep it going,” Mr. Trump added.
Under the deal, Israel receives financial assistance for the purchase of around $3.8 billion in weapons a year.
Since its founding in 1948, Israel has received more than $300 billion, adjusted for inflation, in U.S. economic and military assistance, according to the Council on Foreign Relations, far more than any other country since 1946.
The Israeli premier has said he wanted to end Israel’s reliance on U.S. support.
In June, Mr. Netanyahu called for his country to increase its military autonomy and reduce its reliance on Washington.
In January, he told The Economist that he hoped to do so within a decade, while in May he told CBS that he wanted support to reach “zero”.
Tuesday’s (November 3, 2026) announcement was nonetheless met with backlash from Israeli opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, who said it showed that Mr. Netanyahu must go.
“The fact that Israel’s defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct is,” Mr. Eisenkot said in a statement.
“He can no longer be trusted and must be replaced.”
On Tuesday (November 3, 2026), Mr. Trump cited attacks by leftist Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the U.S. Senate in Tuesday’s (November 3, 2026) midterm elections after harnessing popular discontent and anti-Israel sentiment, as part of the reasoning behind the decision to end aid.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” he said on Fox, referring to Israel and the assistance.

President Trump said today that U.S. military aid to Israel will soon end:
The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday.
The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.
Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel.
***
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Doesn’t Congress have something to say about this? Of course. This is the context of Trump’s rather casual announcement:
In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries.
So that agreement is coming to an end. It is being replaced, in effect, by a cooperation agreement contained in the most recent Defense Authorization Act:
The 2027 National Defense Authorization Act includes a provision that would expand U.S.-Israeli cooperation on the development of new defense technology and identify opportunities to integrate Israeli defense technology into the U.S. military. The NDAA has not yet been approved by Congress.
That provision was the occasion for hysterical misrepresentation by liberals. We wrote about it at the time.
Prime Minister Netanyahu has been saying for a while that this development is in the works. I don’t have a particular problem with it. Israel is a wealthy and technologically advanced country. Its federal budget is around $271 billion, $46 billion of which goes to defense. So our $4 billion is less than ten percent of Israel’s defense budget.
As the Democratic Party has turned anti-Semitic, our modest aid to Israel has become more of a political issue than anything else. Israel can do without it. I think our strategic and technical cooperation is more important, and that will continue.

sources.news_title: Trump Announces $4 Billion Israel Aid Cutoff — And Says Netanyahu Asked For It
sources.text:
President Trump just announced a major change in one of America’s longest-running foreign-aid relationships: roughly $4 billion a year in U.S. assistance to Israel is set to end after 2026.
Trump is keeping the alliance while rewriting who pays the bill.
It is a shift from American taxpayers financing the relationship to Israel purchasing the American military equipment it wants — and Trump says Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu raised the idea himself.
Fox News reported that Trump made the announcement during an Election Day call to “Fox & Friends.” He said the support — which he described as military hardware, cash, or barter — “gets cut off at the end of the year.”
Trump said he and Netanyahu reached the understanding months ago after discussing the issue for several years. According to the president, Netanyahu initiated the conversation and said it would be appropriate for Israel to stop receiving the assistance.
The timing was unmistakably political. Trump pointed to Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s attacks on U.S. support for Israel and argued that ending the payment removes an easy Democratic talking point.
Trump said Israel is a thriving country that no longer needs the payment. He also made clear that the alliance and the ability to buy American weapons will remain intact.
“They can buy whatever they want,” Trump said.
That distinction is the heart of the story.
Trump is separating friendship from dependency. Israel can remain a close strategic partner without receiving an automatic multibillion-dollar transfer from American taxpayers every year.
BREAKING: President Trump says the U.S. will end roughly $4 billion in annual aid to Israel by the end of the year, revealing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed to the decision.
“Because they don’t need it,” Trump said during an exclusive interview on @foxandfriends, describing Israel as a thriving country that no longer requires American financial assistance.
Trump also said Netanyahu raised the idea of ending the aid himself. He emphasized that Israel remains one of America’s most reliable allies as the two countries prepare for a major shift in their financial relationship.
— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 3, 2026
The current arrangement traces back to a deal signed under Barack Obama.
The State Department says the 2016 memorandum committed the United States to $38 billion in security assistance for fiscal years 2019 through 2028. That breaks down to $3.3 billion in annual Foreign Military Financing and $500 million a year for cooperative missile-defense programs.
The agreement was the largest bilateral military-assistance pledge in U.S. history when it took effect. The missile-defense portion supports joint systems that have included Iron Dome, David’s Sling, Arrow II, and Arrow III.
The package was negotiated by the Obama administration but entered its ten-year funding period during Trump’s first term. It represented a long bipartisan commitment, not a yearly favor created by the current White House.
It also explains why Trump’s “roughly $4 billion” figure is accurate shorthand. The existing package totals $3.8 billion per year before any additional emergency or supplemental funding.
A State Department security-cooperation fact sheet explains that Foreign Military Financing gives Israel access to American systems such as the F-35 and supports purchases through U.S. foreign-military-sales and commercial channels. Israel has also used those channels for heavy-lift helicopters, aerial-refueling tankers, precision-guided munitions, services, and training.
The fact sheet says Israel had hundreds of active Foreign Military Sales cases worth tens of billions of dollars as of late 2023. Those purchases can take years to manufacture and deliver, so ending annual grants does not instantly erase the existing defense pipeline.
The old agreement also phases out Israel’s ability to spend part of the financing on Israeli-made equipment. By 2028, the annual Foreign Military Financing allocation was supposed to be spent entirely through eligible American channels.
Much of the aid therefore cycled back into the American defense industry.
Trump’s announced model goes one step further: Israel would use its own money to buy what it needs.
That is an unmistakably America First arrangement. Keep the alliance, keep the defense trade, and stop treating a wealthy partner as a permanent aid recipient.
There are still important implementation questions.
The existing memorandum runs through 2028, and Congress controls appropriations. Trump did not release a written termination agreement during the interview, and Netanyahu’s office had not immediately published its own detailed account of the change.
Those facts do not erase what the president announced. They mean the next step is turning the announcement into the appropriations, notices, and contracts required to make it real.
The Congressional Research Service previously warned that ending Foreign Military Financing would affect existing weapons contracts as well as future purchases. Israel could have to fund those contracts itself, find other financing, or renegotiate obligations that extend beyond a single budget year.
CRS noted that U.S. financing lets Israel stretch payments for major weapons purchases across multiple years. Contracts already signed can remain in the production queue long after the original appropriation, creating potential termination costs for both governments if a deal is simply canceled.
The report also said Israeli leaders had already discussed weaning the country off American security aid. Israel was considering a substantial increase in its own defense spending, while both governments were weighing what a future security arrangement should look like after the current memorandum expires.
That background makes Trump’s announcement less sudden than it sounds. The abrupt element is his year-end timetable, which arrives two years before the existing memorandum’s scheduled 2028 finish.
That is precisely why the new relationship matters.
This goes beyond a symbolic line-item cut. If completed as Trump described, it changes who pays the bill while preserving Israel’s ability to purchase American defense systems.
This would be a start, but…
1) It’s pennies on the dollar. We’ve spent over $50 billion on the War with Iran on behalf of Israel.
2) The same American taxpayer funds will just flow through as military assistance/coordination instead of as a separate line item in the appropriations bills.
3) They spent $30 million against me because I was the only remaining Republican to oppose this foreign aid.
You’d have to be a fool to think they’re going to end this. It’s a desperate Election Day lie.
— Thomas Massie (@RepThomasMassie) November 3, 2026
Rep. Thomas Massie immediately challenged the announcement, arguing that federal support could simply reappear under different programs.
That skepticism puts a useful marker on the table: the public should watch the actual appropriations and defense agreements. A renamed funding stream would fall short of the change Trump described.
But Trump’s stated direction is still clear. A prosperous ally should pay its own way, and America’s support does not have to mean an endless taxpayer-funded allowance.
That is a significant reset — and one that could become a model for how Trump handles other wealthy American partners.
The alliance remains, and the weapons relationship remains.
What changes is the assumption that U.S. taxpayers must always pick up the tab.

sources.news_title: Trump Promises to End $4 Billion in Aid to Israel
sources.text:
Trump Promises to End $4 Billion in Aid to Israel
After nearly two years of generously financing Israel’s military with American taxpayers’ money, President Donald Trump has decided to end that support. Conveniently, the revelation arrived on Election Day.
On Tuesday, Trump announced that Washington would stop providing Israel roughly $4 billion in annual military aid by the end of 2026.
The promise comes as Americans increasingly question Washington’s extraordinary financial and military commitments to Israel. Yet Trump offered no newfound commitment to constitutional limits on federal spending. Instead, he openly acknowledged that the payments had become a political liability for Republicans.
Whether this sudden concern for American taxpayers will outlast the elections is anyone’s guess.
Trump’s Vow
Speaking by telephone on Fox & Friends Tuesday morning, Trump announced that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed to end the payments.
Trump argued that Israel no longer needs American assistance because of its economic prosperity:
They don’t need it.
He added:
Israel is a very thriving country.
Trump insisted that Netanyahu himself had proposed ending the assistance:
I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money…. He brought it up. He said, “I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid.”
The president clarified that Israel could continue purchasing American military equipment without taxpayer subsidies:
They can buy whatever they want.
Trump also presented the decision as a step toward fiscal responsibility:
We’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money. You know, somebody that wants to have a balanced budget. I’d love to be able to balance our budget.
Netanyahu’s office offered no immediate confirmation of the agreement. In January, the Israeli prime minister proposed gradually eliminating American assistance over a decade. Trump’s announcement suggests a dramatically faster timetable.
More strikingly, the two leaders supposedly discussed the arrangement for years. Yet Americans learned of the breakthrough on the very morning they went to the polls.
A “Bad Talking Point”
Trump acknowledged the political calculations behind his decision.
Referring to Democratic criticism of American aid to Israel, he complained:
The best talking point that these lunatics have on the Left.… The Left uses $4 billion payment that everybody knows about, no secret, as a signal of unfairness and we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it is too easy.
The president specifically singled out Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan:
Why? Because they [Israel] don’t need it…. And because why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?
El-Sayed has argued that American taxpayers should not finance foreign militaries while struggling to afford basic necessities at home.
Speaking to reporters in late October, he declared:
I don’t think we should be funding foreign militaries generally…. That’s Israel. It’s also Egypt. It’s also Saudi Arabia and Qatar and UAE.
El-Sayed stressed he favored spending that money on domestic priorities, an argument that, ironically, echoes Trump’s own “America First” promises.
Other Democrats
El-Sayed is hardly alone. Maine Democratic Senate candidate Troy Jackson has opposed continued military assistance to Israel.
In Michigan, Democratic congressional candidate Donavan McKinney pledged to “end the military aid and arms that America gives to Israel.” He defeated a pro-Israel incumbent in the August primary.
New York congressional candidate Claire Valdez has called for an arms embargo and an end to military assistance.
The opposition extends into Congress. In April, 40 members of the Senate Democratic caucus voted to advance a measure blocking a $295 million bulldozer sale to Israel, while 36 supported blocking a $151.8 million sale of 1,000-pound bombs.
In July, 103 House Democrats supported an amendment introduced by Republican Thomas Massie of Kentucky to eliminate $3.3 billion in military financing for Israel. It failed, 104 to 314, with 10 members voting “present.”
The votes underscored growing opposition to Washington’s military commitments to Israel.
Billions in American Aid
The assistance Trump promises to end stems largely from a 2016 agreement negotiated under President Barack Obama. It provides for $38 billion over 10 fiscal years, from 2019 through 2028, subject to congressional appropriations.
The package includes $3.3 billion annually in Foreign Military Financing (FMF) and another $500 million for missile defense.
Under FMF, American taxpayers finance weapons and military equipment for Israel, primarily through U.S. defense contractors. Supporters tout the arrangement as economically beneficial. Yet the transaction remains straightforward: Taxpayers subsidize a foreign military while American weapons manufacturers collect the proceeds.
Congress has already approved the funding for fiscal 2026. According to the Congressional Research Service, lawmakers appropriated more than $4 billion in military assistance and defense cooperation funding for Israel, including $202 million for programs outside the existing agreement.
Meanwhile, Washington and Israel have been negotiating a new security arrangement. As we reported last November, Israel initially sought a 20-year agreement, repackaging military assistance as joint research, weapons development, and production. The Israelis reportedly wanted the arrangement to “include even more in annual assistance.” In May, Israel’s Defense Ministry confirmed formal negotiations.
The regular payments represent only part of Washington’s commitment.
According to Brown University’s Costs of War project, Washington spent $21.7 billion on military aid to Israel and another $9.65 billion to $12.07 billion on related operations across the Middle East between October 2023 and September 2025.
Those figures exclude the separate U.S. war against Iran that began in February 2026. By October 16, the Pentagon estimated that the conflict had cost American taxpayers another $47.1 billion.
Despite Trump’s repeated promises to end costly foreign entanglements, his administration continued supporting Israel militarily and started another war — also because of Israel. Trump’s latest announcement offers no guarantee that emergency assistance or future military commitments will cease.
Americans Sour on Israel
Trump’s announcement comes amid a significant shift in American public opinion.
A March Pew Research Center survey found that 60 percent of Americans viewed Israel unfavorably, up from 42 percent in 2022. Among Republicans younger than 50, 57 percent held unfavorable views.
An October Chicago Council survey found that 56 percent favored reducing or ending military aid to Israel, including 35 percent who wanted it stopped entirely.
A September Marquette Law School poll found that 55 percent believed Washington provided too much military aid to Israel. Only 12 percent considered it insufficient.
Trump’s remarks suggest he recognizes the political problem. He did not primarily invoke constitutional limits, the staggering federal debt, or Americans’ right to keep more of their earnings. Instead, he seemed more troubled by Democrats exploiting the spending in their messaging than by the spending itself.
If ending military subsidies to Israel is the right policy, why did Trump, who campaigned on putting America first, wait nearly two years to embrace it?
Trump’s long record of broken promises gives Americans ample reason for skepticism. With negotiations over a new security framework underway, Washington could simply replace the payments with other forms of military assistance, leaving taxpayers to foot the bill. Until Trump follows through with concrete action, his Election Day declaration remains precisely that: another promise, conveniently timed and politically useful.
