sources.text:
The president says he reached an agreement with Benjamin Netanyahu to end nearly $4 billion in annual military assistance, although Washington could still provide aid if Israel needs it.
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Tuesday that the United States will stop providing its regular military assistance to Israel by the end of 2026, saying he reached an agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to end payments totaling approximately $4 billion annually.
Speaking on Fox News’ “Fox & Friends,” Trump said the two leaders had negotiated the arrangement months earlier and agreed that Israel no longer needed the financial assistance it has received from Washington for decades.
“We’ve already agreed that by the end of this year we won’t be paying Israel,” Trump said, according to Reuters.
The president emphasized that the decision would not necessarily end American support for Israel, saying Washington would remain willing to provide assistance if circumstances required it.
The announcement represents a potentially significant change in U.S. foreign policy, accelerating a transition Netanyahu had previously proposed carrying out over approximately a decade. It also raises questions about how the administration intends to end the payments before the expiration of an existing military assistance agreement in 2028.
Trump Says Agreement Was Reached Months Ago
Trump disclosed the arrangement during a television interview on Election Day, describing the decision as one he and Netanyahu had already settled privately.
The president said Israel had become capable of financing its own defense needs and argued that continued American payments were no longer necessary.
According to The Independent’s Nov. 3 report, Trump also linked the decision to criticism from Democratic and left-wing politicians who have questioned American military assistance to Israel.
His comments suggest the administration intends to end the established annual payments while retaining the ability to provide additional assistance under certain circumstances.
However, the president did not explain whether the arrangement covers all categories of military assistance, including missile defense programs, or whether certain forms of cooperation would continue under a different financial structure.
The White House also has not publicly released the terms of the agreement described by Trump.
The distinction is important because the United States provides Israel with assistance through several programs, and the president’s remarks did not establish how each would be affected.
Existing Agreement Provides $3.8 Billion Annually
Israel receives approximately $3.8 billion annually under a 10-year memorandum of understanding negotiated during President Barack Obama’s administration.
The agreement provides for $38 billion in military assistance over fiscal years 2019 through 2028.
Approximately $3.3 billion annually is allocated to foreign military financing, while another $500 million supports cooperative missile defense programs.
Much of the assistance finances purchases of American military equipment, meaning the arrangement also benefits U.S. defense manufacturers.
Trump rounded the annual amount to $4 billion during Tuesday’s interview.
His announcement raises questions about how the administration intends to reconcile the proposed cutoff with the existing agreement.
Although the memorandum establishes a framework for assistance, Congress retains authority over federal appropriations. Ending the payments could therefore require additional administrative or legislative steps, depending on how the agreement is implemented.
Trump did not identify any legislation or formal changes to the memorandum that would establish the year-end cutoff.
Netanyahu Previously Proposed Ending American Aid
Trump’s announcement follows months of public discussion about reducing Israel’s dependence on American military assistance.
In May, Netanyahu told CBS News’ “60 Minutes” that he wanted Israel to become financially independent of the United States within approximately a decade.
“I want to draw down to zero the American financial support, the financial component of the military cooperation that we have,” Netanyahu said.
Netanyahu argued that Israel’s economy and defense industry had developed sufficiently to begin reducing their reliance on American financial assistance.
He also said he wanted the transition to begin immediately rather than waiting for another Congress.
The Israeli leader initially envisioned a gradual reduction extending beyond the expiration of the existing agreement in 2028.
During meetings with senior Trump administration officials in July, Netanyahu reiterated his desire to eliminate direct military financing over approximately 10 years.
According to The Times of Israel, an Israeli official said Netanyahu wanted to replace the traditional aid relationship with a broader strategic partnership.
The proposal contemplated reducing direct military financing while preserving some missile defense assistance and expanding cooperation on advanced weapons systems.
Trump’s announcement Tuesday suggests the two leaders have since agreed to a considerably faster timetable, although the details remain unclear.
Republicans Had Proposed Replacing Aid With Trade
The administration’s decision also follows an effort by Republican lawmakers to restructure the U.S.-Israel defense relationship.
In June, Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., introduced a resolution calling for a new agreement that would end direct American military assistance and require Israel to finance its own purchases of U.S. weapons.
The proposal received Netanyahu’s endorsement.
According to The Washington Post, Netanyahu expressed support for the initiative during a meeting with Stutzman and Rep. Abraham Hamadeh, R-Ariz.
The Israeli prime minister argued that his country was ready to move beyond its traditional role as a recipient of American financial assistance.
The proposed arrangement would preserve military cooperation while shifting more of the financial responsibility to Israel.
American defense manufacturers could continue selling weapons to the Israeli military, while the two governments would expand joint research, weapons production, and technological development.
U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also publicly supported the concept of replacing direct assistance with a trade-based partnership.
The congressional resolution was nonbinding and did not independently terminate existing aid.
Nevertheless, the proposal demonstrated that some Republican lawmakers were prepared to reconsider an arrangement that had long enjoyed bipartisan support.
American Military Assistance Faces Growing Scrutiny
Israel has received more cumulative American foreign assistance than any other country since its founding in 1948.
According to figures cited by The Independent, the total exceeds $300 billion when adjusted for inflation.
U.S. military assistance increased substantially following the Hamas-led attacks against Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent war in Gaza.
The Independent reported that at least $21.7 billion in American military assistance was transferred during the first two years following those attacks.
The financial relationship has faced increasing scrutiny from lawmakers and voters amid disagreements over Israeli military operations and American involvement in Middle Eastern conflicts.
Some Democrats have advocated restrictions or conditions on military assistance, particularly concerning Israeli operations in Gaza.
Other lawmakers have supported maintaining assistance because of Israel’s strategic importance and the potential consequences of weakening its military capabilities.
Among Republicans, proposals to reduce direct payments have emerged alongside continued support for Israel’s security.
Supporters of replacing aid with trade argue that Israel should finance its own defense purchases while maintaining close military and intelligence cooperation with Washington.
Critics of ending the existing arrangement have raised concerns about the effects on Israeli military readiness, American influence, and regional deterrence.
Trump’s announcement introduces a new timetable into that debate.
Military Cooperation Could Continue
Despite announcing the end of regular payments, Trump indicated that the United States would remain prepared to assist Israel if necessary.
That qualification leaves open the possibility of future emergency military assistance, joint defense programs, or other forms of financial and logistical support.
It also means the announcement should not be interpreted as a complete termination of the U.S.-Israel security relationship.
The two countries maintain extensive cooperation involving intelligence, weapons development, missile defense, and regional military operations.
Netanyahu has previously proposed replacing direct military assistance with a partnership involving joint investment and advanced defense technology.
The administration has not clarified whether Tuesday’s announcement reflects that proposal or a different arrangement.
Nor has it explained whether the end-of-year deadline applies to funding already appropriated by Congress, future appropriations, or scheduled payments under the existing memorandum.
Those questions will be central to determining how the agreement affects both countries.
Major Change Ahead of Existing 2028 Deadline
Trump’s announcement establishes his stated intention to end regular military payments to Israel by December 31, two years before the existing assistance agreement is scheduled to expire.
The president characterized the decision as a mutual agreement rather than a unilateral withdrawal of American support.
Netanyahu’s earlier statements indicate that Israel has been preparing for a transition away from direct U.S. military financing, although his previously proposed timetable was considerably longer.
For Washington, the decision could substantially change the financial structure of a defense relationship that has remained a central feature of American Middle East policy for decades.
For Israel, it would accelerate the shift toward financing military purchases independently while preserving access to American defense technology and cooperation.
The precise consequences will depend on the terms of the agreement and how the administration implements it.
Trump has made clear that he intends to end the regular payments this year. Whether that change also affects missile defense funding, existing congressional appropriations, or future emergency assistance remains unresolved.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Donald Trump said on Tuesday.
The Republican president told Fox News Channel during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.
Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel.
Even far-right conservatives, who have supported Trump in the past, have taken issue with U.S. support for Israel, with prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson openly questioning the value of the relationship.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu’s office. But at least some of his political opponents were cautious.
Yair Golan, a leader in Israel’s opposition bloc, said an end to U.S. military aid would deal a “severe blow to Israel’s security” at a time when the country is fighting wars on multiple fronts. “The burden of funding defense needs at such a critical juncture will fall entirely upon the Israeli public,” Golan, a former deputy military chief, said in a statement.
Tens of billions of dollars have gone to Israel
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years.
In 2016, President Barack Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries.
Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point.
He told The Economist in January that he wanted to “taper off” U.S. military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was “in the works.”
Trump says critics can easily target the $4 billion payment
But the optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point.
“The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” Trump said Tuesday on Fox. “And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.”
Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years.
There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the U.S. has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance.
In addition, much of the assistance the U.S. provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the U.S. economy.
Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, U.S. defense contractors may see an impact.
There was more aid after the Gaza war started
An academic study published last year showed the U.S. under the administrations of President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza war in 2023. The study was published on the second anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict.
Another study, also published last year by the Costs of War project at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs, said the U.S. had spent roughly $10 billion more on security aid and operations in the broader Middle East in the previous two years.
While the reports relied on open source material for most of their findings, they offered some of the most comprehensive accountings of U.S. military aid to close ally Israel and estimated costs of direct American military involvement in the Middle East.

sources.text:
According to President Donald Trump, he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have agreed to end the “$4 billion a year” in U.S. aid to Israel by the end of 2026.
This is the first anyone has heard about this, at least publicly. It will be interesting to see how Netanyahu reacts to Trump’s seemingly impromptu announcement on FOX News’ “Fox & Friends” morning talk show Tuesday morning. The embattled Israeli leader is on the record saying he wanted another Memorandum of Understanding allocating the annual funds until tapering off at the end of “10 years.” He is also embroiled in a live leadership fight in which he may or may not lose his prime ministership.
The annual $3.8 aid package does not expire until 2028.
What is Trump up to here? On one hand, he may be desperately trying to signal to Republican voters on election day that his party is not slavishly beholden to Israel, as a growing clique on his right flank now alleges. Disapproval of Israel — particularly over the Iran war, which has torpedoed confidence in Trump’s ability to steer the economy — is increasing among Republicans. Claiming such a break from Israel now, even if it is just about the MOU, would be a stunning departure from the norm.
Indeed, Trump told FOX directly that it's become a campaign issue. "Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when (Israel) don't need (the aid)?" Trump said, referring to Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.
On the other hand, he might be trying to hurt Netanyahu, who as mentioned above, is in the political fight for his life. His support from Trump has been a net-positive in his own elections. A sudden loss of a guaranteed $3.8 billion in annual military aid — at a time in which the nation is fighting multi-front wars, and is by all measure stretched economically — could be devastating. Security is one issue that spans all voting constituencies in Israel, and a loss in confidence could affect the horse trading for building a Likud-led governing coalition.
But is it all smoke and mirrors?
As we have reported on these pages, and the Quincy Institute folks have written about extensively, the Israelis and their supporters in Washington have been working to shift the aid from the MOU model to the dark labyrinth of the Pentagon contracting system. Through legislation (Section 219), Congress is trying to build a new architecture that will “accelerate the US-Israel defense technology partnership, including technology sharing, coproduction of weapons systems, and bilateral research and development across multiple domains of warfare, including biotechnology, autonomous systems, artificial intelligence, cyberwarfare, and more.”
A designated executive agent will be in charge of the relationship, reducing space for Pentagon and congressional oversight. In other words, the billions in aid will still get to Israel, but in the shadows, making the relationship less politically radioactive. WASHINGTON — The United States will stop providing $4 billion in aid each year to Israel in 2027 but will sell arms to its closest ally in the Middle East, President Trump said on Tuesday.
The Republican president told Fox News during a phone call on Election Day for the midterms that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had approached him about the idea and that they have been talking about it for a couple of years.
Trump said Israel doesn’t need the aid and it’s a lot of money for the U.S. to spend. But Trump also said that U.S. aid to Israel has become a Democratic talking point for candidates such as Michigan U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a vocal critic of Israel.
Even far-right conservatives, who have supported Trump in the past, have taken issue with U.S. support for Israel, with prominent commentators like Tucker Carlson openly questioning the value of the relationship.
“You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash,” Trump said. “Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they don’t need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
But if Trump intended the announcement to make a last-ditch effort to sway midterm votes, analysts said it likely would not work.
“It’s an open question if this was about politics, but it isn’t going to change Republican voters, and it certainly isn’t going to change Democratic voters,” said David Schenker, who served as Trump’s top diplomat for the Middle East in his first term and is now with the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Israeli opposition leaders want to hear from Netanyahu
There was no comment from Netanyahu or his office as of Tuesday evening Israel time, several hours after Trump’s announcement. The prime minister did post twice on social media, but he focused on unsubstantiated allegations of foreign interference in Israel’s elections, not on what Trump said.
But at least some of his political opponents were critical.
His chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, called on the prime minister to speak to the possibly radical change in U.S.-Israeli relations.
“The fact that Israel’s defense establishment is learning of a shift in our strategic relationship through the media, at the same time as the Israeli public, shows just how dangerous Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct is,” Eisenkot, a former military chief, said in a statement.
Yair Golan, a leader in Israel’s opposition bloc, said an end to U.S. military aid would deal a “severe blow to Israel’s security” at a time when the country is fighting wars on multiple fronts.
“The burden of funding defense needs at such a critical juncture will fall entirely upon the Israeli public,” Golan, a former deputy military chief, said in a statement.
Tens of billions of dollars have gone to Israel
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over decades.
In 2016, President Obama, a Democrat, signed an unprecedented security agreement with Israel to give its military $38 billion over 10 years, amounting to $3.8 billion a year. Under the agreement, Israel’s ability to spend part of the funds on Israeli military products was to be phased out and eventually all of the money would be spent on American military industries.
Netanyahu has talked about the need to wean Israel off the aid in the past and has said that the American aid would end at some point.
He told The Economist in January that he wanted to “taper off” U.S. military aid in the next 10 years and that such a change was “in the works.”
Although Trump spoke of ending the aid by the end of 2026, such an abrupt shift would be all but impossible, and Congress will have a large say in what happens. More likely, there could be a wind-down of the current memorandum of understanding if Congress agrees, but it’s unclear if that could happen as early as 2027. The current agreement is not set to expire until 2028.
Behind the scenes, there have been discussions about whether the U.S.-Israel arrangement should be restructured in the long term into one that’s more of a partnership of the two countries’ defense tech and weapons manufacturing industries.
The 2027 National Defense Authorization Act includes a provision that would expand U.S.-Israeli cooperation on the development of new defense technology and identify opportunities to integrate Israeli defense technology into the U.S. military. The NDAA has not yet been approved by Congress.
But there has been some concern from the Israeli side that such a shift in the relationship could result in the Israelis giving up their intellectual property but still facing constraints imposed by the U.S., according to a person who is familiar with the diplomatic discussions but was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
Meanwhile, some critics, including Rep. Ro Khanna, a California Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, have criticized the provision in the NDAA. Khanna said such integration between the militaries would lead to the U.S. losing sovereignty.
Trump says critics can easily target the $4 billion payment
The optics of the aid had also become an issue, according to Trump, who singled out El-Sayed for using it as a talking point.
“The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” Trump said Tuesday on Fox. “And we can’t allow that to happen. I don’t like that, because it’s too easy. It’s almost too easy a target. And Bibi and I have been talking, and we’ve agreed. He was very understanding of it.”
Phasing out direct military and economic aid to Israel has long been a subject of debate in both countries and has gained traction in the last several years. “This has been coming for a long time,” said Schenker.
There are several issues that complicate it, though, not least of which are obligations the U.S. has to Israel under the terms of the Camp David peace accords with Egypt, which require the United States to support Israel and Egypt with security assistance.
In addition, much of the assistance the U.S. provides Israel comes in the form of foreign military financing, or FMF, that gives Israel the money but requires it to spend the money on American-produced weaponry, meaning the funds are plowed back into the U.S. economy.
Unless Israel plans to spend the same amount on purchasing American materiel, U.S. defense contractors may see an impact.
In addition, even if aid were to be suddenly cut off, there would still be many years of previous purchases in the pipeline waiting to be delivered. Most purchases take years from the sale to construction and then delivery.
“The real question for me is whether weapons deliveries will be affected,” Schenker said. “Will Israel be prioritized?”
Finley, Lee and Superville write for the Associated Press. AP writer Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump on Tuesday morning said that the United States would halt billions of dollars in annual aid to Israel by the end of 2026, potentially ending decades of military funding for one of America’s closest allies in the Middle East.
“We were giving them $4 billion. We are. But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” Trump declared during a call-in appearance on the “Fox & Friends” morning program on Fox News. Israel’s 10-year memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the United States, which currently gives Israel $3.8 billion annually, runs through 2028, so it’s unclear how easy it would be for the White House to stop the funding this year and whether Trump is truly committed to changing the arrangement.
“It’s a bad talking point,” Trump said in reference to the aid, questioning why Republicans should have to deal with criticism from hardline pro-Palestinian Democrats like Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed over it. His comments came as Americans across the country are voting Tuesday in midterm elections, including Michigan’s, that will determine control of the U.S. House and Senate.
“If they did need it, I would say keep it going,” Trump said of Israel’s budgetary situation. But referring to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s statement in January that he wanted to taper off aid to zero at some point in the future, Trump said, “we give them more than anybody else and they no longer need it.”
Trump added that he’d reached an agreement with Netanyahu on the issue, telling Fox News that Netanyahu was the one who raised the issue given the Democratic opposition to the continued funding: “He brought it up. He said, ‘I think it would be appropriate if we do not receive aid,’ because he understands that this is one of their points of contention.”
A growing number of Democratic congressional candidates across the United States have campaigned on a platform of reducing or halting military aid to Israel during the run-up to Tuesday’s midterms. This April, dozens of senators — almost all of them Democrats — voted in favor of a failed motion to block the sales of certain weapons to Israel.
Trump also joked about moving to Israel if his political fortunes flag in the United States, telling Fox that he was “at 99% approval rating in Israel” and “if people got tired of me in the U.S., I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister.”
While the Prime Minister’s Office did not respond to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency’s request for comment, Israeli financial and military officials expressed surprise and concern at Trump’s announcement in anonymous comments made to various Hebrew media outlets.
Gadi Eisenkot, the chairman of the opposition Yashar party, the second-largest in Israel behind Netanyahu’s Likud following elections last Tuesday, argued that “the fact that the defense establishment—along with the citizens of Israel—learned of a shift in the strategic relationship through the media, demonstrates just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a real danger.”
Yair Golan, chairman of Israel’s liberal Democrats party, also slammed Netanyahu in the wake of Trump’s statement, tweeting that “precisely at a time when Israel’s defense spending has reached enormous proportions, when Israel needs to replenish its offensive weapons stockpiles, and after air defense capabilities have been depleted following such a long war—Netanyahu logs another massive failure under his name.”
“The cessation of U.S. aid is heavy damage to Israel’s security” and “a responsible prime minister would have fought to increase American aid, not eliminate it,” added Golan.
Similarly, Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman asserted in his own post that “the price of Trump’s support for Netanyahu [is] 3.8 billion dollars a year.”
Former Prime Minister Yair Lapid, for his part, called Trump’s decision “one of the most severe political and security failures in the state’s history.”
“It’s inconceivable that Netanyahu capitulated to it, and even more inconceivable that he failed to prepare the security apparatus,” Lapid declared.
Eisenkot, Golan, Liberman and Lapid are allies in the opposition, which is trying to form a wide enough coalition to oust Netanyahu from power following the elections last week.
Trump endorsed Netanyahu ahead of the election, arguing that his leadership was critical to destroying the threat from Iran. Netanyahu has long campaigned on his close ties to various world leaders, including Trump.
The hawkish Zionist Organization of America, which has traditionally supported Trump, also criticized the president’s move, with its president, Morton Klein, questioning “why the U.S. isn‘t also ending the over $4 billion in annual U.S. aid to the Arab Muslim countries of Egypt, Jordan, Pakistan and Lebanon, and the Palestinian Authority entity.”
However, Republican Jewish Coalition CEO Matt Brooks took a different tack, arguing that under Trump, the U.S.-Israel relationship was “stronger than ever” and that “the process of weaning foreign military assistance to Israel is not unexpected and is something that has been openly discussed in partnership and coordination between the governments of the United States and Israel.”
Brooks added, “Ultimately what will come out of this will be to the benefit of both countries and strengthen our cooperation even further.”
On the other side of the political spectrum, Ilan Goldenberg, the chief policy officer of J Street, the liberal Jewish Middle East advocacy group, tweeted that “2 years ago on Election Day Trump was promising peace in the Middle East. This time ending FMF [Foreign Military Financing] to Israel. Goes to show how much things have moved politically, and simultaneously how much we can’t trust what he says to actually happen.”
Rival pro-Israel lobby AIPAC said that “we support the current MOU, which is set to expire next year. By working closely together, the two democratic allies help keep each nation secure, promote regional peace and stability, and grow both economies.”
Trump’s announcement additionally faced criticism from Brett McGurk, a former senior national security official who played a central role in the Biden administration’s handling of the Israel-Hamas war.
“Obama-era MOU provides $3.3B annually in military financing plus $500M for missile defense. Nearly all of these funds must be spent on purchases from US industry, supporting US jobs. The total is less than one-tenth of one percent of federal spending annually,” noted McGurk in a post on Twitter.
“Phasing out the MOU early is a decision for the President and Congress. It may be time to do so but the debate should start with accurate facts and figures,” he said.
The MOU is not “not legally binding” and the funding must be approved by Congress each year, noted Lara Friedman, the president of the progressive Foundation for Middle East Peace. Accordingly, the issue isn’t set to be revisited until the next budget is presented and then both Republican and Democratic senators and representatives would weigh in.
Michael J. Koplow, the chief policy officer at the dovish Israel Policy Forum, said that in addition to no such budget having actually been presented, it was important to note the timing of Trump’s remarks on Election Day. Republicans are facing several hard congressional battles in places like Michigan, where progressive Democratic candidates are calling to curtail aid to Israel.
“I think he’s trying to say to voters in Michigan, this isn’t actually an issue you should be voting on because the money is going away anyway,” Koplow assessed.
While there is growing support in the United States for cutting defense aid to Israel, there has also been a push among some members to more tightly integrate the two countries’ defense establishments, with a group of lawmakers seeking to include language in the annual defense policy bill that would expand U.S.-Israeli defense technology cooperation.
A section of the National Defense Authorization Act for 2027 would require the secretary of defense to designate an “executive agent responsible for synchronizing cooperative efforts between the United States and Israel, including bilateral defense technology research, development, testing, evaluation, integration, and industrial cooperation.”

Trump says US to end $4 billion annual military aid to Israel this year
sources.text:
Trump says US to end $4 billion annual military aid to Israel this year
US President Donald Trump said Washington would end its annual military assistance to Israel by the end of 2026, following an agreement with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The move follows Netanyahu's proposal to gradually reduce Israel's dependence on US aid over the next decade, as the current $38-billion military assistance package runs until 2028.
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had reached an agreement under which Washington would stop providing military aid to Israel after the end of this year.
Trump said Israel no longer required the funding, which he put at USD 4 billion annually. He added that some Democrats and left-wing politicians had been citing the assistance while criticising Republicans.
In an interview with Fox News programme Fox and Friends, Trump said he and Netanyahu had agreed several months ago to end the annual payments to Israel.
Trump said the United States would stop providing the funds by the end of the year, but would assist Israel if the country needed help.
Israel plans to progressively reduce its reliance on US military assistance over the next decade, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in January. He had discussed the proposal during a December visit to US President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida.
The United States has been providing military assistance to Israel under a 10-year memorandum of understanding (MoU) covering the period from 2019 to 2028. Signed on September 14, 2016, during the Obama administration, the agreement commits the US to providing Israel with USD 38 billion in military assistance over the 10-year period
Netanyahu told The Economist that Israel had matured and built considerable capabilities, prompting him to seek a gradual reduction in military aid over the coming 10 years.
The existing package provides USD 3.3 billion a year in military financing, along with USD 500 million annually for joint missile defence programmes such as Iron Dome, Arrow and David's Sling.
The grants are largely meant to fund purchases of weapons and ammunition. The agreement also requires Israel to spend a progressively larger proportion of the assistance in the US.
Netanyahu's proposal would therefore reduce Israel's dependence on American military support after the current USD 38-billion arrangement, which remains in force until 2028.

sources.news_title: Trump says US will stop funding Israel after year-end
sources.text:
Trump says US will stop funding Israel after year-end
US President Donald Trump says he made a deal with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that the United States will stop funding Israel after the end of this year.
Speaking to Fox News, Trump said Israel no longer needed the $US4 billion ($A5.7 billion) in annual funding and that some Democrats were using the US financial support to Israel as a talking point to criticise Republicans.
"You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash," Trump said.
"Look, we give them $US4 billion of things and money, and they don't need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we've been talking about it for a couple of years because it's a lot of money."
"We've already agreed that by the end of this year we won't be paying Israel. Now we'll help Israel if they need it," he said.
It was a surprise announcement as US voters headed to the polls for midterm elections that will decide who controls Congress.
There was no immediate comment from Netanyahu's office on Trump's remarks.
Trump did not provide details or explain how the funding would be stopped at the end of the year, given that the Memorandum of Understanding that provides $US3.8 billion in US military aid to Israel each year does not expire until September 2028.
The United States has sent tens of billions of dollars in military aid to Israel over the last few years.
An academic study published last year showed the US under the administrations of president Joe Biden, a Democrat, and Trump provided at least $US21.7 billion in military assistance to Israel after the start of the Gaza Strip war in 2023.
The study was published on the second anniversary of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks in Israel that provoked the conflict.
"They can buy whatever they want. So can Europe. We make the greatest weapons in the world," Trump added on Tuesday.
Netanyahu said in a May interview with CBS that he hoped to wean Israel off US military support within a decade.
In a June letter to a US congressman he wrote that the time had come for Israel "to move from aid recipient to partner".
US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza Strip war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats.
A June Quinnipiac University poll indicated 48 per cent of voters and 66 per cent of Democrats believe the United States is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 per cent and 20 per cent when the question was first asked in 2017.
Some members of Trump's Make America Great Again movement have also become increasingly critical of Israel, accusing it of having misled Trump - who campaigned in 2024 on a promise to avoid foreign military interventions - into believing Iran could easily be defeated in a war.
Congress passed a law in 2020 authorising the funding for Israel but the Senate and House of Representatives must still pass appropriations bills every year to distribute and release the funds.
Netanyahu said in an interview with an Israeli television channel in October: "If you think we're going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that's tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won't happen because America has changed."
Support for Israel among Democratic voters has plummeted, candidates critical of Israel are winning Democratic primaries and even moderate politicians are increasingly willing to challenge decades of US support for Israel.
"The left uses the $US4 billion payment that everybody knows about, well it's no secret, as a signal of unfairness, and we can't allow that to happen," Trump said.
"We were giving them 4 billion, we are, but it gets cut off at the end of the year," he said.
"Why? Because they don't need it."
